items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.

items.body_md:
On August 10, CashCall filed a further employment application, Dkt. 49, in Case No. 26-03102 before Judge Barrett Marum in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of California. The docket entry is styled as an "Employ (Application)" — the same procedural form as the Manatt, Phelps & Phillips retention filed at Dkt. 42 on August 5 — but the specific professional or firm being retained is not identified in the docket header, and no secondary reporting has surfaced confirming the identity. What can be said with certainty is that this is a second retention application distinct from the Manatt engagement and from the CRO notice filed at Dkt. 43; the substantive terms, proposed compensation, and applicant will appear in the filed application itself. Classified as substantive but, pending those details, not independently important until the identity and rate structure are confirmed — a contested or richly compensated retention in a case running on roughly $300,000 of interim DIP borrowing would carry materially different weight than a routine professional engagement.

The retention posture matters here because the estate's liquidity position is tight. 
Judge Marum limited interim DIP borrowings to $300,000 — far below the $1.3 million initially sought — and scheduled the second-day hearing for August 26, with the debtor's professionals running without approximately $290,000 budgeted for the carveout account during the interim period.
 Each new professional added to the estate's payroll competes against that same constrained carveout, and the U.S. Trustee has already demonstrated willingness to press on professional fees at the interim DIP stage. 
The debtor is represented by Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, LLP (Schuyler Carroll and Patrick DuBois) as legal counsel, Dundon Advisers, LLC (Matthew Dundon) as financial advisor, and Financial Law Group (Leslie Gladstone) as CRO.
 A third retention — whatever it covers — will need court approval and will draw scrutiny from the U.S. Trustee at or before the August 26 final DIP hearing, particularly given 
the docket's suggestion that the U.S. Trustee's and CFPB's arguments resonated with Judge Marum
 at the first-day hearing.

Dkts. 46–48 — the Schuyler Carroll pro hac vice admission and associated BNC certificates — are procedural and routine; they carry no independent weight on recovery. The next concrete milestone is the August 26 final DIP hearing, at which Judge Marum will rule on the full ~$4 million insider financing facility; the outcome will set the estate's operational runway and, correspondingly, the realistic timeline for any plan or asset monetization that determines creditor recovery.

items.lede: On August 7, the court entered an order admitting Schuyler G. Carroll of Manatt, Phelps & Phillips LLP pro hac vice to represent the debtor and debtor-in-possession (Dkt. 46). The BNC certificate of notice confirming service of that order followed on August 8 (Dkt. 47).
items.body_md:
On August 7, the court entered an order admitting Schuyler G. Carroll of Manatt, Phelps & Phillips LLP pro hac vice to represent the debtor and debtor-in-possession (Dkt. 46). The BNC certificate of notice confirming service of that order followed on August 8 (Dkt. 47). Both entries are administrative in character and carry no immediate consequence for the recovery posture of judgment creditors, but Carroll's admission is a structural marker: 
the order formally seats Carroll — already named as debtor's counsel — as admitted counsel of record in the Southern District of California proceeding
, completing the appearance of Manatt's restructuring team ahead of the August 26 final DIP hearing.

The weightier backdrop is unchanged and worth holding in view as that hearing approaches. 
At the July 24 first-day hearing, arguments from the U.S. Trustee and the CFPB resonated with Judge Marum, who limited interim DIP borrowings to $300,000 — well below the requested $1.3 million — and set the final DIP hearing for August 26, 2026.
 
That compressed interim window means debtor professionals will almost certainly go without a cumulative ~$290,000 budgeted for the carve-out account, and the debtor is riding into the August 26 hearing on thin liquidity.
 The DIP lender is an affiliate owned by the debtor's CEO, J. Paul Reddam — a conflict that drew scrutiny at the first-day hearing and has not been resolved on the docket. The August 26 final DIP hearing is therefore the next substantive event at which the court will determine the full DIP facility terms, the adequacy of creditor protections, and — critically for judgment creditors — whether the lien carve-out structure ultimately shields avoidance action proceeds from the insider lender. 
A related fraudulent-transfer case challenging an October 2021 distribution to Reddam as intended to hinder the San Mateo judgment remains pending, with the debtor's summary-judgment motion having been denied on July 14, 2026;
 the estate's ability to prosecute that claim is directly tied to whether DIP financing survives and on what terms.

The next concrete milestone is the second-day / final DIP hearing on **August 26, 2026** (Case No. 26-03102, Courtroom 2, 11:00 a.m.), at which Judge Marum will consider final approval of the DIP facility and any remaining first-day relief. Judgment creditors should monitor whether any objections to the DIP order — particularly from the U.S. Trustee or CFPB — are filed in the days preceding that hearing.

items.body_md:
The 72-hour lookback window (Thursday–Saturday) produced three docket entries, none of which represents a substantive development. Dkt. 46, filed August 7, is a pro hac vice application and order (CSD 3005) — a routine credentialing entry that signals new counsel seeking admission to practice before Judge Marum in the Southern District of California, but carries no bearing on the recovery posture without knowing which party is expanding its representation. Dkt. 45 (August 6) is a certificate of service, and Dkt. 44 (August 6) is an appointment order — both procedural in character. The identity and alignment of the newly admitted counsel (Dkt. 46) and the subject of the appointment order (Dkt. 44) are not disclosed in publicly available docket abstracts; confirmation would require pulling the underlying filings from 
the case on PACER, No. 3:26-bk-03102 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of California
. Until those documents are reviewed, the significance of either entry cannot be assessed and neither should be read as a turning point.

The appointment order (Dkt. 44) is worth flagging only in context: the U.S. Trustee's August 4 paperless entry declining to appoint a committee of unsecured creditors was already covered. An appointment order filed two days later on August 6 does not fit the profile of a creditor committee order given that decision — its subject is more likely a professional or examiner appointment connected to the professional-employment application at Dkt. 42 (filed August 5, covered in the prior briefing). The 14-day opposition window attached to that application (Dkt. 43, CSD 1180) runs through approximately August 19, meaning any objection to that retention must be filed before the August 26 final hearing. That deadline now sits on the near-term critical path for creditors who want to contest fee arrangements or challenge the scope of the engagement.

The case's structural constraints remain unchanged and continue to define the recovery thesis heading into August 26. 
Judge Marum capped interim DIP borrowings at $300,000 — far below the requested $1.3 million — and scheduled the final DIP / second day hearing for August 26, 2026.
 
The debtor's professionals are operating without the roughly $290,000 budgeted for the carve-out account during this interim period, and by the debtor's own budget the estate arrives at August 26 on thin liquidity.
 
The claim stack consists of approximately $245 million in the De la Torre ("San Mateo") unconscionable-interest class action judgment, approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending enforcement judgment, roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation, and approximately $5 million in trade debt and professional fees.
 
The debtor is a fully non-operating entity: it ceased substantially all lending by 2021, made only 21 loans totaling $94,619 in March 2026 under California's new 36% rate cap, and terminated its remaining employees on June 30, 2026.
 Against that claim stack and those assets, the August 26 hearing is where the case's path — whether a confirmable plan is achievable, whether DIP terms are restructured, and what the creditor distribution framework looks like — will begin to take shape in earnest.

The next concrete milestone is the **Final DIP / Second Day Hearing before Judge Marum on August 26, 2026**, at which the court will consider final approval of the DIP facility and the debtor will need to demonstrate a viable path forward given a liquidity runway that, by its own projections, leaves little margin.
